Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: Samir Rashid was sixty-four when the campaign trail finally stopped him cold. Ten years prior, as a relief coordinator in a fractured Middle Eastern province, he had watched a medical convoy dissolve under mortar fire. The explosion threw him into the dirt, and for hours he lay trapped beneath corrugated metal, the sharp, familiar scent of burning timber and scorched canvas filling his lungs. When rescuers finally pulled him clear, the silence that followed the barrage was absolute, and it was in that vacuum that the militia's radio chatter and the heavy tread of uniformed boots began to make sense. He tried to maintain order, but the strangers who approached his makeshift clinic were as likely to be desperate looters as aid donors, their questions sharp and unanchored. His marriage fractured under the weight of his unspoken dread, leaving him alone in a house that suddenly felt like a trap. Within months of returning to the United States, Samir had retired from fieldwork and transitioned into local politics, yet the war never left his nervous system. Every campaign stop became a minefield. When a constituent leaned across a folding table to discuss border policy, Samir's shoulders locked; the stranger's proximity instantly dragged him back to the faces of armed patrols pressing into his sector. The memory did not arrive as a coherent narrative but as a physiological ambush. Terror flooded him, so thick and immediate that he had to stop pacing the stage and grip the podium until his knuckles whitened. He forced his breathing to slow, deliberately clenching his jaw to keep his voice level, and redirected his attention to the campaign spreadsheets in his briefcase. The overworked hours that followed were not ambition but survival; he buried himself in drafting housing legislation until his eyes burned, using the endless paperwork to keep the images at bay. Yet the terror never stayed buried. Once the workday ended, the quiet of his suburban study would settle over the room, and the unusual stillness triggered a visceral alert that the next strike was imminent. He would rise and patrol the perimeter of his home, repeatedly testing the deadbolts and windows until the metal clicked into place, convinced that any failure would leave him trapped beneath rubble again. The constant scanning of the tree line and the street below fractured his recollections of that day, leaving him with only disjointed shards: a radio transmission here, a plume of smoke there. These fragmented pieces would then pull him back to the edge of the stage, where he found himself hyper-aware of any mention of troops or foreign conflicts, his attention narrowing until only military topics registered. The exhaustion of perpetual vigilance inevitably bled into his coping mechanisms. When the dread peaked, he would retreat to his office and throw himself into committee reports, using relentless overworking to outrun the panic. He tried hard to control his emotions, swallowing the tremors in his hands and masking the tightness in his chest behind a polished demeanor, but the strategies only amplified the underlying alarm. The relentless appraisal of danger then fractured his recollections of that day, leaving him with only disjointed shards that refused to cohere. By refusing to process the fear, he left his nervous system hyper-sensitive, making every pause in conversation feel like a threat and every closed room a potential trap. Eventually, the suppression cracked. The more he distracted himself with administrative tasks, the more the suppressed terror would surface in overwhelming waves, forcing him to abandon his desk and sit in the dark. The more he tried to control his reactions and overwork himself, the more the underlying dread sharpened, turning every quiet room into a potential trap and his constant scanning into a self-fulfilling prophecy. He was certain that if he ever lowered his guard, the silence would return, and this time there would be no rescue. The loop had tightened his chest until he could no longer distinguish past from present. He came to therapy after a town hall meeting spiraled when a reporter asked about foreign aid funding. Samir had stared at the man, unable to look away or respond, convinced the conversation was a prelude to violence. Now, he sits in a quiet office, hoping someone can help him untangle the wires before his own vigilance isolates him completely.
